utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Amongst the accused, Drago Nikolic is not present and we have had a filing, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Mr. Nikolic will not attend proceedings today and we will do everything that he will attend as of Monday. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have a waiver just for the record. The other accused are present. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Madam Nikolic, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, today it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. The witness is present. Mr. Zivanovic -- I take it that there are no preliminaries. I'm not asking for any. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we left it off with the mass graves of Nova Kasaba 6, 7 and 8. I will go immediately to the grave number 8, since I saw that in the previous two there were only one or two bodies. I went through the findings of your report, between the pages 51 and 71 in the B/C/S, or 44 to 65 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be 1D1070. I saw that in those findings, I believe there were precisely 24, you mentioned therein that the injury may have been caused by a shot from a distance as a part of the combat. I will cite an example from one of the findings, which is page -- I think you have that in B/C/S. We only have it in English here. This is page 57 of your report. There is a comment of yours that the description of injuries is a correct one and that it corresponds with the finding. However, you say that the cause of death can be discussed and you conclude by saying that the injury could have been caused from a shot from afar, as part of combat. What did you base that conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion or comment I provided contains two parts. The first part refers to the principal injuries and we go back to the autopsy report where the injuries were described in detail. It is an example of a proper explanation of the injuries as required by the profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, I anticipated the interpreters making an indication to you. Please slow down and do not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the injuries precisely described therein, and hence my comment that this was a proper description of injuries. However, what prompted me to make the conclusion that it may have been as part of combat from afar was the fact that the projectile was stuck in the scapula and in the upper thorax. This indication, that is the projectile being left in the body, is the proof telling us that it arrived from afar or with reduced energy. A projectile fired from a firearm, for example a rifle, and yesterday I mentioned what the speeds are, slows down the greater the distance. A projectile fired from up close would have gone through the body for sure. A projectile could be slowed down when encountering an obstacle along the way before hitting the body. It can be slowed down by any means and then it remains in the body. For that reason, I said that may have been an injury caused by the war as part of combat. I mentioned that as a possibility given that it arrived at a somewhat reduced speed and it remained in the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, when one says as part of the war conflict, that would mean that it was fired from a certain distance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we are discussing the distance, as I mentioned yesterday, it was not determined here. No analysis was conducted. As the reporters themselves say in the collective report, they say that they did not analyse the distance of firing pursuant to some standard forensic elements used to establish the distance between the rifle barrel and the body itself. That is why I commented a part of the final report by Mr. Haglund when he said that the projectile could have been fired point blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If there was a possibility that the projectile was fired from a distance, can you tell us approximately what the distance could have been?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to rely on theory now. For a firearm or rifle, anything beyond three or five metres with such weapons is considered a distance, given that there are no gunpowder traces left on the body. For side arms, hand guns, with a short barrel, that distance is over 100 centimetres. That is the distance between the barrel and the body. If less than that, one can find gunpowder traces. The research conducted by Professor Popov from St. Petersburg, and I contacted him personally, as part of the research he managed to detect gunpowder traces at distances greater than 40 metres. This surprised me greatly. I wasn't aware of such a possibility. And he explained to us that a projectile travelling through space and the part towards the bottom of the bullet sucks in a certain amount of gunpowder which then arrives at the body itself as well. To be precise, any distance greater than the range of gunpowder particles fired from a rifle is considered a distance which probably would not leave any trace on the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you're discussing distances from the point of view of gunpowder particles and traces. However, I'm interested in the other type of distance you've been talking about, which has to do with the fact whether the wound is only an entry wound or an entry/exit wound. In other words, whether the bullet had left the body.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This type is quite important as well and it depends on numerous factors. If one finds a bullet in a body, without the bullet having hit an important bone, such as the femur or pelvis, one of the greater bones, as well as some other bones, which can slow it down ... for example we have an example here of the bullet hitting the scapula, which has the ribs on one side and the soft tissue on the other, projectiles fired from a rifle usually go through the scapula. The fact that it remained inside the scapula points to the fact that it had lost sufficient energy for it to remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this answer of yours, can one estimate the distance of the firing of a bullet which failed to penetrate the scapula?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking from the point of forensic medicine, it is very difficult. One would need to carry out additional analyses that have to do with gunpowder particles and we could have to know some other elements which I, as a forensic medical expert, can take into account, say at the place where the cartridge was found, et cetera, and in that context, one can try and assess the damage that could have been caused by such a bullet if there were obstacles in between or to try and come up with another explanation as to why the bullet had slowed down. What I know from my practice is that projectiles fired from the same firearm had different ranges and which very much depended on the humidity of the gunpowder, the type of charge, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that there were some 24 reports there. They are all similar in terms of contents and with the same conclusion. I suppose that your explanation regarding all of those reports concerning the possibility of the injuries being caused by -- as part of combat, would be approximately the same. Of course, I can cite the pages precisely and we can have a look at all those reports, if needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go through these reports. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at the next report. Let us have a look at the report which is at your page 58, and we are about to see it on the screen. We also have an injury to the chest. Could we please have a look at the main injuries?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] the report said the display is disclosed to us yesterday. It is at our -- on our exhibit list, just a moment. It is CD -- CD from 25th of June 2008. It was wrongly marked as 24th of June 2008. And all these documents are from this CD we got from the Prosecution yesterday. Yes. ERN number is X0046006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just clear the record. This was material that was given to the Defence years ago that we assisted them in finding in the record so we have just given it to them. This isn't some sort of late disclosure, just so you're clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We just got the English translation of these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we only have the English version on the screen, but you have already explained the main injuries and that is what I wanted to focus on. In your comment at page 58 of your report, it says that it also could have been caused by combat, especially with a view of the projectile's remaining in the body.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your explanation for the position you took regarding this autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have an injury to the thorax and a part of the projectile, we have three bullet fragments in the lower and upper arm. We have a characteristic injury to the thorax and in the arm. The direction of the projectile was from the front to the back. The fact that the fragments remained in the soft tissue mean that the projectile had defragmented either when hitting the bone or by hitting an obstacle before reaching the body. In any case, it is characteristic of the injury, and taking into account the nature of the injury to the thorax, we have certain indications as concerns the distance, and that is what made me conclude that it could have been caused by an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next report, X 0046021, page 3. That is the next report, the next autopsy report in your report. Page 59.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And on the next page, it is also stated that the injury may have been caused during an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have again injuries to the thorax and the limbs, as well as the hip bone. There is also a bullet fragment in the chest and in the pelvis, as well as in the lower right leg and the left femur, the left thigh. We have projectile fragments here, which means --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I was told that there was a technical difficulty in the documents being brought up to the screen. I hope a couple of minutes will suffice to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a problem that is going to be solved soon, Madam Registrar? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The problem has been solved, it seems, Professor, so may we continue or rather could you continue with your answer. I apologise, I interrupted you. Perhaps you don't remember where you left off.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right, thank you. This is a properly described injuries in the autopsy report and how they are defined and described. And from these descriptions obviously they are injuries of the extremities, limbs, and the thorax, caused by firearms and projectiles or, rather, elements of the -- of injuries that can be caused when firing is from a distance, in view of the fact as in previous cases that in the tissues and fractures, parts of the projectiles were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now move on to the next page, 6040, I think the number is. That is also to be found on page 59.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have the Serbian version, please? It is case number 50, so next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. You don't have it on your screen, or rather you might have the English version on your screen. But I think that is to be found in your own report.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 59 of your own report, body number 50.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation is the same as in the previous case. The injuries have been correctly defined and described, the head, the trunk or chest, and the limbs, and here we are dealing with a number of radiographically established fragments, bullet fragments, and casing fragments, which indicate that fragmentation occurred either when the bullet hit a bone or through previous fragmentation, but in any case, in these bodies or the bodily remains or remains of the tissues, these elements were detected which can indicate that the bullet came from a distance, that the projectile came from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you look at the next report straight away, please? It's on that same page, and that's 6068. Can you explain your conclusions here, please, as far as distance is concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What was found here was a number of fragments, although the radiography findings shows a bullet near the rights shoulder. Now, when it says, "Bullet," I assume he means projectile but when you actually say bullet that is the whole thing with the casing, but what is interesting to note here is a fragment of the bullet in the soft tissue of the left leg in the vicinity of the left femur and a bullet fragment within the skull itself. This fragment within the skull itself is interesting for the following reasons. Bullets very rarely are found in the cavity of the skull you, unless they are lodged in the skull bone itself and the thicker structures of the bone, and it doesn't say that here. However, part of the bullet in the skull also indicates that the injury was caused or that that part of the projectile was very slow or had fragmented beforehand, which once again leads to the conclusion that we are dealing with an injury from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just an explanation. When you say a fragment, do you mean a bullet fragment, a metal fragment, or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, "A bullet fragment," whereas I assume that it's the casing or the metal part, because with the word "fragment," that means that it was completely separated and that that is why it lodged there. So all these elements can indicate distance again and an obstacle within that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next case also relates to your conclusion that this injury was possibly caused during a conflict, X0046085, 46085, on page 4. Main injuries described, the cause of death and so on.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this. It is case number 65. There are several things that need to be stressed here. First of all, that the remains of the skull are almost stripped, that is the outer description, and there is saponification or putrefaction of the lower extremities. The skull was shattered. That's the general description. And radiographically it was established that there was a metal fragment of the bullet in the left femur. The injuries are described and the conclusion made is that in the area of the skull, that there was no reconstruction, it was later reconstructed, and that there were evident fractures linked up with injuries caused by buck-shot, gunshot. In addition to this injury in the skull area described in this way, there is the -- another fracture of the pelvis and the left thigh bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conclusion it says that there are multiple fractures to the trunk and extremities caused by firearms. They are injuries caused by firearms but most probably there are two possibilities, injuries in the head area, the skull, and that some of the shot or parts of the projectile injured the pelvis. Yes, I'd like to apologise for speaking a little fast. The observation that a bullet fragment was found in the left femur tells us that the bullet was fired most probably from a rifle or that kind of firearm. So it's one projectile. Whereas the injuries described in the head area, in the area of the skull, and the elements found, indicate gunshot. So that this injury, or these injuries, and the different types of injuries, can indicate, may indicate, injuries caused during combat, and the fact that the projectile has lodged there means that it was an injury from a distance. And the third point that I'd like to stress here in this particular case is that the remains of the skeleton were almost bared and that on the lower extremities, the limbs, there was a certain type of putrefaction which is known as saponification. Now, in correlation with the skeletisation and saponification, if we look at one of the bodies and see that a complete skeletisation has taken place and that on the other there is saponification, this might mean that the body was exposed to different environments, a normal environment, in a grave, or in the air, and saponification, whereby the lower extremities where the saponification was noted, that those limbs might have been in a humid environment where humidity was dominant which once again can indicate the fact that the body was exposed to humidity in one area and then later on that the body might have been buried with decay and putrefaction taking place, although saponification is also found in humid grave sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned gunshot, buck-shot. Can you tell me, on the basis of your experience as a forensic expert, whether perhaps that indicates any specific type of weapon having been used?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Buck-shot -- well, it wasn't described in detail, that is to say the injuries caused here, and buck-shot is used in weapons where the casing has a charge with metal balls. Usually they are circular balls, round balls, and they can differ in size, small, minute ones and big ones, and calibration according to the size of the pellets, so whether the, as the small pellets or larger pellets, they cause similar injuries to the bones such as the skull. So if you reconstruct the whole situation, then you can see that there are regular circular holes with a broader areas, broader channels, on the internal wall of the flat bone which is what the bones of the skull are. So we are able to determine localisation with great precision and this is done through reconstruction, which they did in this particular case, and this was done very pedantically but not described in the same way because the number of injuries are observed, but here, in this case, no fragments of gunshot were found in the skull, although the observation and conclusion made is that the injuries were caused by buck-shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to X 0046119, the next case. That's on page 61, 104 -- body number 155. Not 155. 55. You also observed that this could be an injury caused during combat. Can you explain why? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The injuries are in the head area, they are divided into the head area, the trunk or thorax and the limbs or extremities, the left -- or rather right arm and right leg. X-rays find fragments in the left knee, in the pelvis and left foot, and like in the previous cases, the possibility exists that these injuries were caused by firing from a distance and that these parts of the body were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find the next case, although it's similar but let's go on to body number 57, 616 -- 6156.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it was concluded that the whole body was skeletised, or practically the whole body, and at the joint -- there was a lot of soft tissue in certain parts of the body and the joints were separated. It doesn't say which areas soft tissue remains. This indicates that certain parts of the body had decayed more than others and that the lack of soft tissue means that external factors, in this case animals, had affected the body. There are fragments of the bullet casing in the chest and head, left elbow and in the region of the leg. Now, the injuries to the trunk or chest were found in the left third rib in the mid-clavicular line and a deformed sharp-pointed bullet jacket in soft tissues attached to the trunk. That's what the description says. The limbs, probable gunshot injury to the left forearm, fragmenting the upper thirds of the radius and ulna and with bullet metal fragments found adjacent, which means that this particular fragmentation is just an observation that was made, and I can accept that because if it was found in the soft tissue, that that's -- that a projectile caused the bone fragmentation. And now this speaks of injuries to the trunk, without observation -- observing the fragmentation of the arms. So this description is partially correct but once again indicates the possibility of the injury being caused from a distance, especially where we come to the trunk where the projectile was lodged in the region of the third rib.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can now move on to the next body, which is body 58. 6153 is the number. Can you explain this, the grounds for your conclusions that -- of the possibility that the injury was sustained in combat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any case, we have the jacket or a small fragment in the left part of the chest, a small fragment in the area of the left leg, and a small fracture on the lower part of the leg which can indicate the distance, or that the projectile lost its force or velocity because it passed through an obstacle prior to hitting the body, and then it is noted here, something which I don't actually understand, that the skull is intact while the pelvis is much better preserved. I don't know what that exactly means. I don't know if it's a mistake in the translation or something but that's what it states. In any case, my answer would be in relation to this question that you put, that a fragment of the projectile remained in the tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are going to move immediately to body 62. 61 is a similar description but it's not in the system so we will move to 62. Fragment bullets or shrapnel is mentioned here, so I would like you to comment on that and of course comment on the conclusion that the injuries were caused from a distance.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have here are the remains of a practically bare skeleton with saponified tissues. It means that these several cases were in similar conditions when these putrefactory changes occurred. There were some metal fragments of bullets in the chest area. That's what it says, and that there was a bullet in the skull. However --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This was too fast for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreter is encountering difficulties, Mr. Dunjic. If you could slowly repeat what you have just said, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Trial Chamber and to the interpreter. I began to reed the text and I don't believe that I don't need to bother you with that but I'm just going to give you a direct answer. We have multiple metal fragments in the trunk. Description of the main injuries refers to a projectile fractures and damage in the skull area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did that lead you to the conclusion that is given here in the finding?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This led to the conclusion that the injury was inflicted during combat possibly and that it was inflicted during combat and that projectile remained in the body, but the found metal fragments, as described in the chest were not noted anywhere except in the radiographic part. Actually this is not recorded in the autopsy report, the content found in the body indicating distance and the possibility that the shrapnel fragmented even more due to the action of some explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move to the next report, please? This is body 63. In your report it's 6227. Can you tell us what led you to conclude that the injury was sustained in combat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have it here that in the radiographical findings two pellets were found at the right foot and around the right knee and small metal fragments near the right femur or in the soft tissue remains of the right thigh. It means that the projectile remained in the body. It indicates the type of weapon, and the injuries that were described in the skull probably indicate that it is quite likely that the irregular opening at the back of the skull is probably an entrance hole caused by a bullet. A specific hole of exit cannot be recognised. So based on that analysis I made my own comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move to body marked 64? This is 6241 in our documents.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, we have a completely bare skeleton, and the skull was shattered and there was an oval hole in the mid-region and a large part of the parietal region was missing and there were also injuries to the pelvis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 5910 now, please? This is actually body number 42. In your findings, it is on page 55.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This case, number 42, also indicates that the skeletal remains were saponified and the tissues were saponified. The body was better preserved in the pelvic region where there is some disintegrating muscle tissue left. There are multiple small perforations on the shirt from undefined buck-shot. The fluoroscopy indicates that there was a fragment close to the right and the left forearm, a small fragment and pellet close to the skull, a pellet in the trunk area, two smaller fragments in the pelvic area, the left thigh -- and the left thigh close to the pelvis and a deformed bullet in the body. As for the injuries, there is a fracture of the 7th rib, where there is a clear bullet hole to be seen. And as for the limbs, there is a fracture with multiple bone splinters in the lower third of the left humerus, above the elbow, close to the elbow, and there is nothing more of a detailed description there. These injuries are obviously buck-shot injuries, with a broad dispersion. When I say "broad dispersion," this is a significant fact for us indicating that when we establish the range of fire with buck-shot wounds on the basis of the pellet dispersion, so the pellet dispersion by their direction and the way they are shaped at the ultimate point, because it is a reverse cone shape, the top of the cone is the barrel mouth and then the pellets disperse in the shape of the bottom of the cone, and that can affect a larger area. So on the basis of that pattern, you can calculate the distance between the rifle barrel and the target. Sometimes you can have more pellets deep in the wound and less on the periphery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are going to move now to body 67, which is on page 68 of your findings, and that is 6298 in our documents.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is case 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, case 67. I would like you to tell us the basis for your conclusion that the injury was sustained during combat.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, there is a skull damage here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's a misstatement of Professor Dunjic's report. He says it's a possible injury in armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I told it it is possible injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. Anyway, it's clear enough now. So let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Possible injury were in confrontation.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the injury is possible in that way, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, it's a small misunderstanding. Can you please tell us what your conclusion is based on that this is a possible injury sustained in conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides the fact that there are two metal fragments, a large skull fracture could have been caused by a fragment or small fragments of metal projectiles which had lost their penetration force and that at the same time they could not -- they were stopped by the body, so again you have the possible distance and extensive injuries. I explained yesterday how it was possible to cause a minor injury at a small velocity with a small projectile and that after the body decomposes and is found, it looks like major damage to the skull or a large fracture because of the state of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to move to body 71, and that is on 6334 in our documents.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are remains of a practically bare body. The skull was shattered. There is a metal fragment in the lower jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what led you to the conclusion in this case that this was possibly a combat injury?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a head injury by a projectile, which was stopped in the mandible, the lower jaw, meaning that this can indirectly indicate distance and as well an injury that we encounter in armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, now we are going to move to other autopsy reports. They are no longer possibly combat-caused -- refer to possible combat-caused injuries. We are now going to look at body 73. Our number is 6367. This is on page 70 of your findings in the B/C/S version. Can we please look at the cause of death? It's noted here that the cause of death is unknown. Can you please tell us if this description and the conclusions from the autopsy could lead to this finding?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is said in the case of 73, which is from Nova Kasaba number 8, confirms that the conclusion, where it says the cause of death has been correctly derived in terms of what was noted in the report, and there is no description of the injuries in the report. It just states no fractures, no skull perforations, no neck injuries, and only on the trunk it is noted that one rib was fractured, which means that this conclusion had to be what it is. There were no obvious injuries. They were not noted in the soft tissue, and I underline that again we have a body that was in the stages of saponification and, as I said yesterday, saponification is a process that indicates that the body was in a humid environment. What is missing here, other than the description, they said that the head was intact, is that the fist or hand was missing and then it would have been proper to describe the putrefaction changes in more detail and to describe more in detail if there were any soft tissue damages or damage in the part of the body where the hand was missing or if there was any damage in the area of the rib fracture. In either case. So when we are talking about the hand, we would need to see the edges of the tissue because then we could determine whether this was caused by animals or some other type of trauma, just as we can see in saponified flesh, if there is an injury or if there are discolourations in the soft tissue which could then indicate that the injuries were inflicted post-mortem. The way it is written here, the conclusion about the cause of death is quite accurate in relation to the report of that -- about that particular body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the last autopsy report from this group. It is body 74. It follows in your report. In our document it is 6382.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bullet core and jacket fragments found in the right upper arm. As for the main injuries, we have comminuted fracture of right temporal bone with pieces pushed inwards. Then pelvis fracture of right pubic symphysis. There is no left pubic symphysis as probably meant was the right pelvic bone. It is a wrong description. Then we have a gunshot injury to the left upper arm, fragmenting the middle third of the humerus. However, the conclusion based on the findings is that it was impossible to prove what the cause of death was. They stated what the injuries are. However, they did not say whether they were pre or post-mortem. And there is a gunshot injury mentioned to the left upper arm and based on that the pathologist was unable to conclude what the cause of death was. My conclusion is that the cause of death is correctly described compared to the findings, although the findings in a segment are imprecise and insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain your comment provided at page 71, which has to do with the entire location of Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having studied the entire location of Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3, and the single case of Nova Kasaba 4, as well as 6, 7 and 8, I analysed this individually, I underlined the correct portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. [In English] 621, English page 65. Sorry, it is not P621 but it is number of page 65 of his report in English. And number of his report is 1D1070.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at the entire location of Nova Kasaba 1, 2, 3, the single case of Nova Kasaba 4, and the remaining locations, 6, 7 and 8, there are differences in the forensic approach of those who did the autopsies and provided descriptions, as I've already stated. In the individual analyses. What is a prevailing characteristic is that there is no consistency between the conclusions and Mr. Haglund's comment. We saw in the individual cases what the inconsistency is between the conclusion and the trauma reports, as well as the relationship between the cause of death and type of injuries. I have to state here that -- that the conclusions concerning the manner of death were arbitrary. May I go on? The conclusions about the cause of death were arbitrary. Here, and in the introductory part I explained that the cause of death could have -- and the manner of death could vary in terms of types when discussing violent deaths and non-violent deaths. In all the cases here, it was mentioned that they met a violent death. The injury itself, if described properly, can be acceptable, but to claim that the death was a violent one, I need to provide precise parameters that point in that direction. In the absence of that, I cannot make any conclusions on the cause and manner of death unless I am required to state my position once I have seen all the facts. It is frequently done in individual analysis when one deals with several aspects of suspicion. Therefore, I stated that the conclusions were arbitrary concerning the cause and manner of death. In particular, in the cases where we have multiple injuries by shrapnel, et cetera. The description of injuries in the case of Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3 is disastrous. It is somewhat more precise with the remaining locations, these being 6, 7 and 8. The established number of cases is correct. The methodology of exhumation and record keeping is fairly accurate. As for the documenting the autopsies, this was carried out properly and according to the protocol. Another thing one has to say about the three locations has to do with the time of death. Based on the given descriptions of putrefaction and changes caused by putrefaction, I provided my comments concerning external and internal examinations and based on all that it is not possible to establish the exact time of death. Certain explanations provided by Mr. Haglund are more or less acceptable, but they have to tally with the other data arrived at once DNA identification is complete and once we have personal identification. We need to compare all the information we have with the date of disappearance, the identity needs to be confirmed, and then all that needs to be cross-referenced with the data contained in the autopsy reports, the putrefaction changes, anthropological characteristics. It is only then that we can arrive at a precise time of death. We cannot do that given the descriptions in the autopsy reports alone. Based on that, it is impossible to establish a time of death, in particular, since we had different degrees of putrefaction in different cases. As regards the cause of death, I've already commented that in the introductory part, I explained what cause of death is, and irrespective of an injury to a head or thorax or a leg, the skull trauma in itself is but a mere fact. However, because of the skull trauma, the cause of death can only be ascertained after it was ascertained that the skull injury was -- occurred in life. Pre-mortem, that is. As regards the mechanism of injury, it is difficult to establish it, even when we have evidently good descriptions, primarily because of the putrefaction we encounter and because we cannot establish the entire length of trajectory. When talking about the issue of whether the person -- a person was killed from afar or point blank, it also has to do with ballistics, forensic analysis of weapons, traces found on the body, direction of firing, as well as based on the noted injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of your report, inter alia you mentioned the international classification of ... Could you please explain in detail what sort of classification it is? It is Exhibit 1073. It is a Defence Exhibit. I think we only have it in English. Could you please tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the international classification of diseases and injuries, there is also a classification in chapter 20. There is a classification of injuries concerning armed conflict. Anyway, they are specified quite precisely. In this forensic description of injuries, one should ascribe every particular injury the exact code from this classification. It is up to the Court to determine the cause of death. The only thing we can do as forensic expert is to classify the injuries precisely according to the standard. We are there to determine whether the injuries we encounter are, for example the injuries contained here under Y35.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Y36.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They begin with Y36 and the subitems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the type of injuries in armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is Y36 to Y36.9.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, Y36.2, we have war operations and types of injuries. This continues in Y36.3 and .4. It would have been far better to have used this international classification of injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While on the topic of the international classification of injuries, can you tell us who drafted it, who created that classification?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's an international standard, accepted by all countries, all physicians irrespective of whether they work with living patients or whether they are pathologists or forensic experts like myself, we are all obliged to abide by the classification in terms of types of injuries, cause of death and the morbidity. The classification exists as to have the same criteria and that anyone can monitor given types of injuries and causes of death across the board, in all -- on all continents. This was drafted so that we could monitor statistically the occurrence of different types of injuries and diseases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that actually answered the question, which was who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're right. Mr. Zivanovic, please, if you could bring the -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you know precisely what the name of the organisation is that drafted this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- excuse me, let me finish. Do you know for how long these rules have been in existence? For example, in your domain? Had they existed before you started working or after that? Is that something you encountered when you began your career?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I started working -- well, I don't know what edition or what revision there was at the time, but it existed already. I believe I began with the 7th or 8th. I believe this is the 10th. There is an entire book in existence with the explanations on how to fill in the data required. I really don't know who published it. All doctors got the same book. And we need to use it to assign codes so as to have level criteria when making diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that we downloaded this from the web site of the World Health Organisation, as indicated on our 65 ter list or rather the list we forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, if we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean temporarily?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Temporarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was quite sure of that, Mr. Zivanovic. We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. I heard you're going to try and finish in the next 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, tell me, please, or rather let's move on to the Pilica locality, which is incorporated in your report, and in the English version it is from page 66 to 92. And in the B/C/S, from 72 to 93. It is Defence Exhibit 10701. Or, rather, 10701 D. Could you tell me, please, whether in this locality, of the autopsy reports that you received from this locality, whether you studied all the findings, all the reports, or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't study all the autopsy reports. I looked at 52 cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us which cases you looked at and which you didn't?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not study cases where the conclusion made was that ligatures existed, and that for the simple reason that I considered, and that's what I wrote in my report, that persons with ligatures can be considered from the forensic aspect with documented injuries as having been executed in one way or another. And that is why I took the cases where this was not concluded. And the reason why I selected the cases I looked at is the same as the ones before. I looked at the forensic aspects, the ways in which the injuries were observed, dealt with and verified, and so for that reason, I analysed those cases in greater detail, in order to establish whether there are any differences, similarities and so on and so forth. As you were able to note in what I said so far, I was very precise in analysing the individual cases to show where the forensic report was -- autopsy report was done forensically correctly, where the description was forensically correct, and where any other pathologist of my type would be able to conclude what type of injury was sustained. Now, at Pilica which was a primary grave site, as I say I selected those cases and looked at them, and generally speaking, for all of them, there is a common denominator or common conclusion, if I can put it that way, and that is that the pathologists working on these cases and in describing the traumas sustained, in fact just set a diagnosis of the injuries, just like in Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3, so when the injuries are -- when it is injuries caused by projectiles, and every forensic expert would not be able, from those descriptions, to test and ascertain whether they really were injuries sustained by projectiles. So that is my overall general conclusion. They deal with skull fractures, for example, as well, and describe them, without more specific diagnostics and descriptions. A separate case that I'd like to set aside here is the description or rather under inconsistencies of the conclusion made based on those descriptions is the case number 38, Pilica 38. It is on page 78 of my report, 01493296, the ERN number. [In English] It's page 147.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here all, all I can do is read it out once again so that we can all hear. The head is missing, the body is incomplete, but the base of the skull is present, putrefaction and saponification. And in the description of the injury, it says, fracture of the skull and fracture of the right part of the pelvis, and the cause is inflicted by firearms. So you can't test the cause of death through the description provided. So this is the inconsistency that I mentioned earlier on. Furthermore, in the entire analysis of this particular case, and this primary grave site, which I conducted, I quoted, at the end of the individual analyses, the report of Mr. William Haglund, and I'd like to dwell on just two points in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's P642, 624, sorry.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his report, he states the following: "The distribution number and angle of hits as well as the other characteristics of the wounds indicate that it could be a burst of gunfire that caused the injuries. There is additional injuries from bullets to the heads of a number of victims indicate that fire was opened from the absolute vicinity or point blank." From this quotation it we can conclude that there was a burst of gunfire and that there were -- that there was additional wounding. From the forensic aspects I cannot -- I'm not able to confirm that. A burst of gunfire implies the firing of a large number of projectiles into a body and this observation is then checked out and verified through an autopsy. What Professor Lawrence in one of his reports did, and I'll be quoting this later on, well, he said very precisely the concentration of injuries and wounds on a -- one body can indicate that the injuries were caused by bursts of gunfire so a forensic expert knows what a burst of gunfire means and how it can inflict injuries. On the other hand, if you have a burst of gunfire, continuous shooting, this implies that the injuries and the projectiles that were found are identical or similar, and this brings us to one thing here. We have one conclusion made by anthropologists, I'd like to stress that, whereas the autopsy finding is unable to verify that. The second point is this, and I'd like to underline that from the forensic aspect, and it is -- he states that very decisively and resolutely, and this cannot be accepted from a forensic aspects, and that's his observation that additional wounds from bullets to the head in many victims indicate that a fire was opened either from a close range or point blank. This observation is incorrect in two ways. The first is that it was up close or point blank, injuries sustained point blank or from absolute -- an absolutely close vicinity, are not described and it implies that traces should be found, that is to say gunpowder particles, whereas the observation that these -- this was a case of additional wounding by bullets implies that the anthropologist, the forensic expert, had established the order in which the injuries were sustained, which is absolutely impossible on decayed, skeletised, decomposed bodies, so as a forensic expert myself, forensic pathologist, I'm not able to determine the order of injuries sustained, especially if there were a number of injuries. I cannot establish their order on the body. I must have precise parameters for me to be able to tell the Court that one injury was first as opposed to the others and which was the last injury and all the injuries in between. That means that the last injury in the series can have the character of being an executive fatal injury, it could be a slit to the neck or it could be firing at point-blank range, but you can't prove that, and you especially cannot prove it with material like this, that is to say autopsy reports and descriptions of the kind that I looked at here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you check whether we are following the correct document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. Yes, we didn't say the page of this document, but the witness explained the part of his report. It is 1D1070. It is English page 91 of his report, 91, as far as I know. It is -- just a moment. It is from page 89 to page 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, in English, we have from page -- it is almost the same, from page 89, I believe, to page 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your report here, I found three cases in which the cause of death was unknown. Would you look at those reports? It's now document 624, Prosecution document 624, and the page is 35, 36 and 37. Or rather 38. And refers to corpse number 9. In your report, it is on page -- your page 74.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. This is an incomplete body with the head, trunk and upper extremities and spine missing, and decay and saponification had set in, and the skeleton was partially bare. The injuries weren't identified on the other parts so the cause of death was not established, so that can be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at page 131 to 133 of that same document. And it relates to body 33, and it's on your page 78. Or 77.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular case, we had the entire body with putrefaction, saponification and decay taking place and a partially bare skeleton, without any precise description of the putrefaction that had occurred. Of the injuries, it is noted that the left pubic bone was shattered when a projectile, high-velocity projectile hit the body. I'm not going to comment on that injury because that's the diagnosis there but the cause of death is undetermined, which would be in keeping with the findings as they have been set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last case from that series is page 279 to 281. It is body number 74, and on page 84 of your report is where we can find it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a case where the body was incomplete, no missing -- missing skull, left clavicle, bilateral upper and lower extremities, pelvic bone, left scapula, all cervical and lumbar vertebrae and 11 thoracic vertebrae. Putrefaction and saponification had occurred and cause of death undetermined and that is in keeping with the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we are now going to take a look at bodies 83 and 84 from your report. They are not on e-court, although the fourth volume of this report by Dr. Haglund, they are there but I don't know whether we have them, we don't seem to have them in e-court, but we do have it on a CD, so that's what we are going to show. Page 3462 and body 83. It starts on page 85 and continues on page 86. Let's take a look at page 33 now of the English version. [In English] "Recovered evidence bullet from right side of jacket." [Interpretation] Can you explain to us what this means?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bullet on the right-hand side of the jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, what -- what does it mean, bullet from right side of jacket? What does that signify? How do you interpret that? Bullet from right side of jacket.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is -- interpret it the way it's written, meaning that it's the entire bullet, the jacket and the projectile, in the pocket of the jacket or in some part of the jacket. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the next body? This is body 84. It's on the following page, and I would like us also to look at page 37.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we have the presence of projectiles and it says bullet in the left side of pocket of trousers. It's the same thing. The bullet is in the trousers, in the clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the pocket of the clothing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the left side pocket of the trousers, which means that the entire bullet, which has not been fired, was in the pocket of the trousers. Usually when you describe the bullet you would say a projectile, a jacket or the projectile, so here the way it's described would indicate that it was a complete bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Thank you very much. I'm now going to ask you to move to the Zeleni Jadar locality, Zeleni Jadar 05. That is also in your report, 1D1070, English pages 93 to 104, B/C/S pages are from page 94 to 104. Generally, can you tell us anything that has to do with -- can you please tell us generally about Zeleni Jadar 5? Your remarks generally, what you have to say about that locality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say first, just like I said yesterday, Zeleni Jadar 5 is a secondary grave. I did not have enough time in order to completely process all the cases, so I just arbitrarily picked 20 cases which I analysed here in order to be able to get a forensic impression about the process and methodology of work generally, since this is a secondary grave, that is linked with Glogova 2. 150 corpses in total were found and I analysed 20 of the autopsies out of that number. According to the report, one body was found at this location with ligatures. No bodies were found with blindfolds. This location, and the remains found there that were examined, there were cases where shell fragments and shrapnel was found in the bodies. What is important for a forensics man is that there was a kind of discontinuity in the development of the putrefaction on these bodies, or, rather, there are bodies that are in advanced stages of decomposition, there are practically skeletonised and there are some corpses that have preserved soft tissues with only a degree of putrefaction. Again, I would like to note that the degree of putrefaction was not described in detail in the autopsy reports, but if you find two groups of corpses with such evidently different stages of preservation, then you have to put this together with the fact or realistic assumption that what is happening here is that we have two groups of bodies, skeletonised bodies, which probably reached that phase earlier, before they were buried in this particular grave, or that the condition in the grave were drastically different. Since this is a secondary grave, we have to take this into account, that the skeletonised bodies, without soft tissues, could have been dead earlier and exposed to conditions that speed up the process of putrefaction, and then later, when this grave was formed as such were in the grave itself as such, because if there are decomposing bodies in the grave already, then we can draw the conclusion that the Zeleni Jadar 5 graveyard already contained some bodies which went through the usual process of decomposition. This is something that I can say about that. Another thing that I can note, which was also noted by Professor Lawrence or Dr. Lawrence, is that some bones show marks of burning or scorch marks in the sacks and also there is charring of the clothing which would indicate that the bodies that were charred and where the bones were also -- seemed to be charred were exposed to a high temperature that can be seen or that is created during an explosion of explosive devices such as shells and other weapons, hand grenades, which is then consistent with the finding that grenade and shrapnel materials were found to a large degree at this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For purposes of illustration, I would like us to look at a couple of reports from this location. We would now look at 33428 on -- in your report, it's on page 96.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is case 189 if I'm not mistaken. And here we have the presence of shrapnel and grenade so the injuries could have possibly been caused by shells and shrapnel, possible shells, the injuries described, even though they are not described in detail, are such that they could have been caused by such objects. Thus, in spite of the brief description, we could come to the conclusion that those are injuries of that nature. In other cases, I described that in such situation it's possible to create the conditions for the development of a high temperature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 3451 now, please? In your comment you said here, and this is on page 97, that it is possible that this injury was caused during combat. Generally, can you tell us what you base your conclusion on about it being a possible combat-inflicted injury?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just in previous cases, I said that shrapnel discovered in the area of the left hip, where there is a large surface that can hold back or stop shrapnel or metal fragments would indicate the distance, and thus can be then connected with actions resulting from combat because shrapnel can be a large object that is created when larger lethal means are fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at your report on the previous page, page 96 of your report? At the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, main injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's trauma related to death in English version, after second paragraph, it reads, "following discussion, these were concluded to be post-mortem injuries." [Interpretation] I would now like to ask you to explain to me how you understand this sentence, in following this discussion you could come to the conclusion that these were post-mortem injuries. I did not actually point this out in some other autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, this remark that is written here also causes dilemmas for me and it makes me begin to think, and I can possibly provide a very broad answer here. What I mean to say is this: When you determine main injuries, and this is how they are noted in the way that they are noted, then this sentence can say that what occurred was a conversation among a number of persons, the pathologist, the anthropologist and so on, and that the conclusion was reached that these are post-mortem injuries. However, the cause of death indicating injuries caused by shrapnel and gunshot wounds would then not be consistent with such a conclusion because then that cannot be the cause of death. It would mean that the injuries were -- occurred after death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much. Now I would like to move to the last grave that you analysed. It's Ravnice 2. So also can you please tell us if you analysed all the autopsy reports of the bodies found in this grave or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case as well, I had to, because of the time considerations, analyse just a number of cases. In this case, that is 20 cases. But I took this locality into account in my analysis for specific reasons. These bodies were actually found on the surface, so throughout the whole time until they were discovered and until the autopsy was carried out, the bodies were on the surface, which would then indicate a different way of putrefaction and the changes that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just did not yet mention the page of your report that this can be found in. This is 1D1070 of your report -- actually, that's your report. And the page in the B/C/S version is 105 to 121, and in the English version it's 105 to 122.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general remark that can apply in this particular case is the following: That the description of the trauma is insufficient and inadequate and that the cause of death was established on the basis of such a description. This would be a general remark. The second thing that can be said about this particular case is that because of this inconsistency, the description of the putrefactory changes, in most cases this is skeletisation or remains without any soft tissue, so in the majority of cases that I quoted we are talking about diagnoses given as descriptions of the trauma, so it is not possible to check if these are actually injuries that occurred. The third thing that needs to be said is the remark that there was shell material that was found there, shell fragments, in certain cases, although there is also a very accurate description of wounds or injuries, which would then correspond to the conclusion that these were actually, in fact, gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like us now to look at a part of the report of 1D1203.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the first case on page 105. This is body number 287. I apologise, I didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a completely skeletonised body. It was exposed for a long time to putrefaction, which is -- which corresponds to the place where the body was found. Fluorographically tiny fragments of metal were found in the remains, these are head and neck injuries here, with only two pieces remaining. And there are no obvious bullet defects on the frontal and left parietal sections of the skull. There are fractures of the single rib present at the angle and then further wounds are described. The cause of death is unascertained. It was not possible to ascertain the cause of death. So this is an accurate conclusion in terms of the elements on which it was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at Exhibit 1214? 1D1214. This is body number 319, on page 106 of your report. It's at the bottom of that page. It is said here that diagnosis -- cut and dried diagnoses were given?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, incomplete description of injuries and a superficial report on gunshot injuries, with the conclusion that there was -- the injuries were sustained by firearms, so cut and dry diagnoses are provided without describing them first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another autopsy report, 1207. It is page 109, body 92.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have skeletal remains without any tissue left, which tallies with the place and time of finding of the body. Radiographically speaking two bullets were found as well as shell material with an addition of multiple metallic fragments in the rest of the body. Description of injuries, as such, points to the injuries which would correspond with the found shell material, although the cause of death only mentions gunshot injury of the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Next page, radiography report. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first page of the summary portion of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It looks like it's on the first page. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radiography, please. We can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the last paragraph of the summary, the last sentence. That is what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion was that the injuries as provided, with an incomplete description, could have been caused by shell material and in the way described. However, in order to verify any gunshot wounds in the sense of a projectile being existent, it is simply not there in the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, concerning the conclusion you made, I believe you've clarified that sufficiently. Therefore, I won't ask you about that. But I wanted to ask you the following or perhaps a colleague of mine will ask you about it. I would like to go to one part of your comment, at page 126 of your report. It is 128 in the English. You mention a report from San Antonio, which contains certain conclusions and recommendations. It was drafted by a professional body that deals with forensic medicine and it took place between the 14th and the 19th of November, although I'm not sure we can see the month in the English translation. First of all, generally speaking, what was your source?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report quoted in my report is something I received from a colleague of mine who is also a forensic pathologist who also provided opinions in certain case, Mr. Zoran Stankovic. At the time he was the head of the military medical academy and also testified here in a case. I quoted that report in my report, so as to provide an illustration of the type of work when they began working in the locations concerning Srebrenica. You can see for yourself that these are statements of certain participants, for example Mr. Gallagher, Yvonne Milewski, David DelPino, commenting upon the work of Mr. Haglund, Kirschner and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about numerous omissions, professionally speaking, in the work they performed. The statements of the people you've just mentioned, do they corroborate your assertions? Could such omissions have resulted in the inconsistencies you have been addressing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can conclude that from my entire testimony. The superficial way of describing obviously points to several things, one of them being the experience of the pathologists doing the autopsies, provided that these were indeed forensic pathologists, many of them were young save for the few who managed the task, who were indeed professional pathologists. And this tallies with what I've been presenting here yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us see the integral part of the report, which is 2D70, page 5.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see a complaint in item 12. I don't think we have that in B/C/S. It is only in English. In any case, it reads that she is complaining that she was instructed how to list the cause of death by Dr. Kirschner. Is that method allowed, to instruct someone carrying out an autopsy, even if the instructor is a forensic expert, is it correct to tell another person what should be the listed cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone is responsible for their work individually, irrespective of who the head of the team is. Only the person doing the autopsy is the person responsible for what they write, and I will illustrate that with the following. Mrs. Helena Ranta, who worked with my team on the cases from Racak, she did not meddle whatsoever with the work of Ante Pintila [phoen], who was a forensic pathologist. His conclusions can be found in the autopsy report. Therefore, recommendations of that nature to change a finding or a conclusion is impermissible for the person signing the autopsy report. To exert such influence is unprofessional. One can provide advice, explanations by senior to junior colleagues, and professional explanations and proof can be given, but to change something that is already written is unprofessional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 13, it says that anthropologist Dorothy Gallagher saw problems in the field and in the lab and that she stated that Dr. Kirschner changed autopsy reports and instructed her what to do while processing them. Is something of that nature allowed, permissible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may have a moment. First of all, it is impermissible. I am pausing because there is an assertion which I quoted in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell it in your own words?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It confirms, I believe it was in a collective report, and I believe it was Mr. Haglund that I quoted, he himself confirms that, that they worked in agreement and under Kirschner's management, or, rather, according to his directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is not whether it is so or not but whether it is permissible. Could you perhaps address it from that point of view? From the point of view of professional work, when doing an autopsy.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing concerning exhumations. In item 13 as well, Ms. Dorothy Gallagher says that Dr. Haglund dictated too much speed in exhumation, and because of that there were shortcomings. Is there a rule in existence when doing exhumations at what rate, speed that should be done, in what way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standards are set according to the circumstances in the field. The pace can have an impact on the evidence, parts of bodies exposed to putrefaction that could be lost in the field. Documentation following from that is also highly suspect -- can also be suspected in terms of its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Item 14 has to do with David DelPino, a Chilean anthropologist. He says that operations were halted when Dr. Haglund was away. What sort of an impact could that have had on the exhumations and autopsies, since the work was halted due to an absence of a member of the team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can have an impact if it's an open-air location, if there is no soil covering the bodies, one only enhances decomposition, changing the pathological substrate substance that needs to be recorded. The bodies that are being exhumed and put in body bags used to transport them to a refrigerator, even during that short interval, one greatly enhances the rate of decomposition. In such cases, later on, you may establish skeletonisation which may not have existed at the place and moment of exhumation, and they halted the entire operation while the bodies were on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another matter concerning item 14 and something David DelPino discusses therein. He says that clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though some contained identification. I'm not precisely sure what it means, but tell me this: According to the rules of your profession, is it permissible to discard clothes found during exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single piece or item of clothing found at a location can be discarded. That is to say, if such clothing is on the body, it goes with the body. If something is found next to the body, say a hat, it can be joined with the body, but if we find pieces of clothing further away or torn, they are still taken and marked separately so that later on we can provide material for additional identification. Say there are trousers. You can't find ten male trousers and then later on suspect that there was a woman among the corpses. If you find clothes, irrespective of where and how it was found, without it you won't have all the indicators and parameters that should and must help you in the process of identification. The DNA analysis carried out is not -- are not the only parameters used to identify the persons found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One of my last questions has to do with this document as well. It's page 12. This is the one. Page 12, and let's look at point 9. Let's look at the title first. It says, "Recommendations, committee recommendations." That is the professional body that looked into all the complaints. So let's focus on point 9 and could you comment on that point, please? It says, "There was too much subjectivity and not enough objectivity when the exhumation and post-mortem examinations were carried out." No, I'm sorry, that doesn't seem to be it. I do apologise. It's page 11. We need page 11. That's right. And it says, "There was mutual agreement on management problems on the part of the supervisors." Now the points are set out and I was quoting from point 9. [In English] "There was too much subjectivity and not enough objectivity in the performance of the exhumation and post-mortem examinations." [Interpretation] Tell me, please, looking through samples, look at these findings at random, do you share that opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I said, it follows it would appear that I'm in agreement with the conclusions made by this professional body. I've just found it. And I have to say that this is linked to what was previously stated about changing conclusions and findings in one way or another, and Haglund in his document for Cerska, the 15th of June 1998 on page 11 of the translation in Serbian precisely noted that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you incorporated that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says the autopsy examinations were conducted under the supervision of Robert Kirschner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just give us a page reference, please? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on page 122 of my report, where I state my opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] 122, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General conclusion on page 122.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
