utterances.text: That's the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is now. Next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 is the relevant paragraph. I'm going to read it out. "In that report, Mr. Haglund states the following, among other things. Autopsy examinations were carried out under the supervision of Dr. Robert Kirschner, director of the international forensic programme of Physicians for Human Rights, and in brackets, [PHR]. Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports was facilitated by ICTY legal adviser Peter McCloskey, the pathology summary was authored by Page Hudson, MD. So from this we can see that certain corrections were made, adjustments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Now, I have first on my list as a co-defendant summoning this witness the Beara Defence team. Mr. Ostojic, do you wish to examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Dunjic, and as you know my name is John Ostojic and I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara in this case. I've had the pleasure to meet you but good afternoon to you again. Sir, I'd like to follow up on a couple of questions my learned friend asked on direct. First and foremost, can you tell us, when you said that it was impermissible to do certain things, why would it be impermissible from a forensic pathologist's standpoint to discard for example clothing or items such as identification found on a corpse?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's just proof and evidence that that forensic pathologist is working very unprofessionally and superficially and I've already said what finding even one item of clothing or fragment of clothing means with respect to the identification of a corpse, of a victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us under what circumstances, if any, would a reasonably prudent independent forensic pathologist permit or allow a Prosecutor or a Defence attorney for that matter to participate in formulating the cause or manner of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There is no evidence whatsoever in the record that any Prosecutor took part in the formulating the cause of death. This is this absurd fantasy that they try to spin off on last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment on that or do you wish to move to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's a misstatement of the facts and I think my learned, friend with the most respect, is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. If we are going to discuss this I don't want it discussed in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Instead of -- because time is always of the essence, I would like to get back to it but I'd like to turn to an exhibit first with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'll restate the question perhaps after this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we have 2D70, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's page 11, the one that you were just looking at, Dr. Dunjic, you were asked specifically about paragraph number 9, and what I'd like to ask you about is paragraph number 6. Let me know when you've had that in front of you. And I'm not sure the extent of your English, but I'll try to read it for you here verbatim. Okay. Paragraph 6 in this report, it says, "Universal agreement on the alteration of reports and final opinion as to the cause and manner of death without consulting the prosecutor who had performed the post-mortem examination, this should not have been done."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you capable of understanding this paragraph, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Under what circumstances, if any, would a reasonably prudent independent forensic pathologist allow or permit, if it occurred, for a prosecutor to participate in formulating the cause or manner of death?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, there is no indication whatsoever that any prosecutor in this case ever took part in any form or manner of death or took part in any autopsy or anything like that, and that's -- it's absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision by majority is to proceed with your next question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what effect, if any in your opinion, does it have on the report if someone other than the forensic pathologist was formulating an opinion as to cause or effect of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I said yesterday and indeed from what I said today too, it is obvious that in all cases, that the observation exists that the cause of death was linked to the injuries, which were either incompletely described or not described at all as having been caused by firearms, and in the manner of death, that what is mentioned is killing. So if somebody keeps insisting upon the fact that we are dealing with killings, with murder, and if somebody keeps insisting but is inconsistent in their findings with respect to the cause of death, then that's quite clear. So a forensic pathologist cannot allow his findings and his reports, particularly in the conclusions about the cause of death, should be altered in any way, just as we must not allow any arbitrary conclusions as to the cause of death, because forensic pathology is very pragmatic in that area. And Mr. Clark in his report indeed addresses this and Mr. Lawrence here too. They were very resolute in stating that you need proof and evidence of the injuries to be able to establish the cause of death. So unless you establish all this, you can't do that, you can't alter something as you go along and then make your own conclusions. So as a forensic pathologist myself, that would be impermissible. I would not accept anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, Dr. Dunjic, that's just not your standard, that's actually the universally accepted standards for forensic pathologists, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- it should be a universally -- it should be a universally accepted standards but quite obviously people have accepted the guidelines and advice, and that is why at the big conference in San Antonio where the leading pathologists and forensic experts and anthropologists meet to debate and discuss matters, they discuss this too. In our own circles, our own professional circles, not linked to these events in Srebrenica or anything like that, our chambers, chamber of forensic pathologists and so on, we discussed that and my information tells me that they discussed it in England, in London, the professionals in their professional circles, discussed this too, how these reports should be written, what you should include and so on. Because as a forensic pathologist, in order to provide you, the Court and lawyers a precise and objective findings and report, that is my duty, and then if you put together all the other parts of the puzzle and all the other elements on the basis of witness testimony and so on, you can create your own picture. I can't lead you to a conclusion which is not substantiated by my report. If somebody was killed by a projectile, then that projectile and everything surrounding the event must be described, and I gave you examples of how we worked. I worked on a large number of cases, an enormous number of cases, of bodies, corpses, which had been putrefied, and then you list everything, you say the corpse has been decomposed, that there were such and such injuries. You don't go and write the cause of death straight away. You have to make those conclusions on the basis of objectively observed facts and recorded facts, and not to say what you assume happened, and then ultimately it's up to the Court to weigh all the evidence and make their decisions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And those findings, I think as you stated to us yesterday, are both -- they come from the external and internal findings that a pathologist conducts during autopsy, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. You must have the external and internal findings, detailed ones, and this refers not only to trauma but to the entire findings and report in which you can describe and see post-mortem changes on the corpse, their degree and all the other processes that can be observed and described on a corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help us understand this, sir. I know there is obviously a difference between cause of death and then manner of death, as you've described and isolated for us today and yesterday specifically on page 62, but when you discuss cause of death and you find that it was "not established," under what circumstances can a reasonably prudent forensic pathologist come to any conclusion as to the manner of death if again, just so you know, the cause of death is "not established"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a subjective position, then, absolutely subjective, because without -- if you cannot determine the cause of death, and this is confirmed by an autopsy report or the descriptions given, and then that you go ahead and conclude that it was a killing, so that's your own personal attitude, subjective, or suggested, a suggested position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me understand this. Are there different criteria or words that a forensic pathologist such as yourself and those universally would use if they are uncertain as to what the findings results should be? And for example if I may assist you, do pathologists, forensic pathologists use words such as unascertainable or uncertain or questionable in their field of specialty when it comes to both cause of death and/or manner of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In rare situations, when you have a fresh corpse and when no clear cause of death is found, whereas you have the corpse, the body, as a fact, then the pathologist can write and state that the cause of death was not ascertained and possibly to explain why, to give reasons why, because there is no evidence of trauma, of disease, laboratory findings are such that they cannot confirm whether there was a metabolic disturbance or whatever, that's one type of situation. And another type of situation is this: When you don't have elements which would indicate that the injury was sustained during life. For example on various organs, the brain, the heart, the abdomen, that would be then linked to the cause of death later on. So we write down that the cause of death in such cases cannot be ascertained because there were changes that took place during the life of the person. And all this has to be written down. Now, if I understood you correctly and your question correctly, I said what the origins or cause of death means and how the person was killed and the injuries that were observed, whether they could be linked to violent death or sudden death or suicide, so this notion of killing is a legal concept. Forensically you have to have certain elements present which emanate from an autopsy and autopsy report, which to a greater or lesser degree of probability indicate to the Court that it was one or another type of injury. And when you say that it is a killing, that a killing has taken place, then you need to substantiate that very well with your arguments for the Court to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was just trying to focus on words such as unascertainable, unquestionable, and uncertain, but what about words -- do pathologists, forensic pathologists, such as yourself in their either cause of death or manner of death use words such as inconsistent with, for example, homicide? Or consistent with homicide? Is that in essence what you're saying, that the pathologists should have noted where they felt the factors were supportive of any one or another conclusion? Isn't that the essence of your work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all cases, well, autopsy and an autopsy report, must be very precise and exact. Somebody can have a large number of injuries, for example, and nobody can challenge that, of the head, the trunk, the limbs and so on. This large number of injuries must be substantiated and documents and then linked up to the cause of death. Now, the manner of death, the manner of death, is something that the pathologist -- it is not up to the pathologist to determine, or he must use an international classification that we saw a moment ago on the manner of injury. Now, it's up to the Court, let me state this again, on the basis of all the evidence presented, to determine what ultimately caused the death of the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we will talk about those classifications since you brought it up. When we discussed the classifications that you've looked at, are you familiar with, and we have used the word interchangeably unfortunately throughout this trial, words such as ambush, but I think one of the OTP witnesses, Richard Butler, identified that ambush as we've have called it as a legitimate military engagement and I think in using the classifications that you did, did you find that those classifications when talking about operations in a war theatre are actually, as you've so identified, legitimate military combat engagements?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, because when it comes to legitimacy and whether something is legitimate, that must be established by lawyers and courts. All I can talk to you about is injuries, the injuries sustained in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this since you have a classification in front of you. Doesn't it use the word "legal" when it does those classifications in war operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Do you wish to explain further or shall we hear Mr. Ostojic? Do you agree that it is leading, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's really directing him to that specific area but I think we saw it on the ELMO but I could do it obviously without leading, if we could have that exhibit, please, now, pleased on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is also going well beyond this witness's expertise as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is what I actually had in mind when he put the first question, which the witness made clear already that he couldn't answer. But he beat me on time. So now it's my turn. I think you need to move on to your next question. And leave this subject matter aside because this is not his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if I may, with the highest of respect to Your Honours, this is specifically identified in his opinion and the expert witness has relied specifically on these classifications, he's noted them, the Prosecution has had them, all I want to do is because he's a pathologist and he may believe that he's not rendering an opinion based on any legal issue but it's clear that these classifications given to pathologists universally they do denote specifically that which I asked the witness, utilising that very word, "Legal".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we are unanimous on this, Mr. Ostojic. Let's move to the next subject, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, when we talk about the cause of death and manner of death as two distinct items, I think yesterday in your testimony you said that basically the two go hand in hand and I think it's in -- on page 51, line 7 through 12, but I wasn't sure on your answer, and if you could clarify it for me, could you have a cause of death that is known but a manner of death that is undetermined or unknown?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are such cases. For instance, when you have the cause of death, I don't know what example to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll give you one. Let's say there is a gunshot wound to the head and you're not certain from the evidence that you've seen whether it would have been as a result of a homicide, a suicide or justification in self defence, for example, or for that matter, a legitimate military engagement. Under those, circumstances, for example, could you determine as a forensic pathologist what the cause of death was but not know what the manner of death was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm going to object to that for foundation, manner of death --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think you need to have a consultation between you and Mr. Mitchell as to who is going to continue the role of Prosecutor with this witness. So I suggest we have a break now. You know what the practice has been. We allow one, unless there are certain circumstances. If you wish to sit near Mr. Mitchell and -- but we prefer if it's only one counsel that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, and it will be Mr. Mitchell and we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's have the break now, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that Mr. McCloskey liked my idea or suggestion. Let's continue, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you repeat your question so that we'll hear the objection again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There has been quite a few but I'll repeat the last one before the break and then maybe we'll deal with that. Sir, before the break I asked you to in essence describe the difference between cause and effect and manner of death and I stated on page 56 as follows, because you had stated you didn't have an example to clarify, could you have a cause of death that is known but a manner of death that is undetermined or unknown, let's say there is a gunshot wound to the head and you're not certain from the evidence that you've seen whether it would have been as a result of a homicide, a suicide or justification in self defence, for example, or for that matter a legitimate military engagement, under those circumstances for example could you determine as a forensic pathologist what the cause of death was but not know what the manner of death was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, he needs to define the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Define the term in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's a legal term, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand it, it is basically he's asking the witness to confirm that as a pathologist, as such, he's not interested in the -- in whether it was a justification in self defence or military engagement, et cetera, but then he adds also suicide and homicide. To my knowledge, forensic pathologist will go into that and that's one of the most fundamental tasks that he has to carry in, short of other evidence, he would need to confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think, with all due respect, we can stipulate if the pathologist can't reach a legal confusion then for that matter if that's what my learned friend is saying, I think the pathologist reports that are in evidence should be stricken if that's what he's saying, but I think a forensic pathologist can indeed reach a conclusion based upon reasonableness and specifically those external and internal factors that Dr. Dunjic has testified to in the last two days, but I'd be happy to stipulate to that if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I were in the witness's place, I know how I would answer that question. But, Professor, would you -- one moment, yes? Why don't you let him answer it? I think he's a perfectly qualified person, coming from a country that in medicine has had a reputation of excellence for decades and decades. We are not talking with someone who doesn't know his subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, if you could please illuminate us on this complicated, seemingly complicated issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I'm glad that you've noted that I come from the country but from a country with an institute with a very high reputation and we have a long tradition and unfortunately experience in matters like this, so my specific answer to your question is that we forensic experts establish the cause of death so we note everything. As for the manner of death, is the wound that is seen, is it quite legal? Actually not that term, not that term legal. Did it happen accidentally, was it a suicide, was it a killing, was the source of that wound that? Then the Court defines the problem for us and says, "Based on these elements that you have noted in your autopsy report, can we talk about a specific manner of death?" I cannot directly answer that question because such an injury can be caused in three different ways, accidentally, it can be a suicide or a killing. In order to be able to give a more specific answer, we can do that and then the Court can draw the conclusion about the manner of death, whether it was accidental, a suicide or a killing. I need to make a very good autopsy report. I need to note or report all the traces which would point to the first, second or third element. I would need to have testimony of witnesses which could indirectly confirm that line. I would need to have the complete records. And then finally my conclusion would note that elements, for example, in the right temple, perhaps that would be an entry wound and an exit wound would be at the left temple, then this would need to be absolutely documented with gunpowder traces but still that would not be reliable evidence that this was perhaps a suicide. It could also be an accidental killing or a murder. I need to provide the Court information based on which they, on the basis of the entire body of evidence, could determine whether it was this or that. I can note that the person was right-handed, that there were traces of blood or gunpowder, that on the entrance wound, there are traces of blood and I could say most probably in the right hand, it was touching the right temple, that's where the entry wound was, et cetera, et cetera, based on which the Court would then draw the conclusion that this could then amount to a suicide, an accidental killing or a killing. As forensic experts, we cannot give final decision on the -- we can provide information about the manner of wounding, but we cannot say whether this was a self-inflicted wound, as an accident, as a consequence of an accident or as a consequence of something else. I cannot say that. So I cannot speak about the legitimacy of something. It's absolutely out of the question that we state opinions on any legal points or whether something is a legal point or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I recognise that, thank you very much, Dr. Dunjic, for that. And so that's why we would use such classifications as you've seen because that lists out specifically what instances you as a forensic pathologist may or may not rely upon in determining whether or not certain deaths that were caused resulted from certain circumstances; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, doctor, we have talked about two specific things here and I just want to separate them for a moment. We are talking about cause of death and manner of death and I started out by asking you if you have a cause of death that is unknown or unascertainable, I think it was your opinion that you could never then make a conclusion as to the manner of death. Now I'd like to look at the opposite. If you do know the cause of death, can you also have the manner of death to be unknown, unascertainable?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The opposite situation would be the same as the one before. I'm never going to say anything about the manner of death, even if I do or do not have the cause of death. The cause of death, when we are speaking in principle, means whether it's an accidental death, a suicide, or a killing. But I'm not going to speak about that if I don't know what the cause of death is. The cause of death could be natural or violent. What are the elements pointing to a violent death? So that I could then determine the manner of death, whether it was a killing, suicide or an accidental death. I would not go into that at all, especially if I'm not aware of the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that but I don't know if you're following me and I apologise to you and the Court for that. What I'm suggesting to you, sir, is that we can have -- if we have an unknown or unascertainable cause of death, in all instances, when the cause of death is unknown, the manner of death should also be unknown or unascertainable, in 100 per cent of the cases?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll restate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Under what circumstances, Dr. Dunjic, could you possibly have, as a reasonably prudent forensic pathologist, under what circumstances can you have cause of death to be known or unknown and manner of death to be known?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the manner of death, whether it's accidental, a suicide or a killing, I can just give my opinion on the basis of precisely established findings only on condition that this is something that the Court requests us to do. The Court could say, "You have the established wounds that are such and such, the cause of death is established. Could this injury be caused by point blank or fire at a distance and would this indicate this kind of wound infliction or a different kind of wound infliction?" So perhaps I can give my opinion to the Court, but it could not be the only opinion of an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But can you in any circumstances conclude or give an opinion, and I respect that, that you are giving an opinion, can you give an opinion as to manner of death under any circumstances if you don't know or have already determined that the cause of death in -- is unascertainable or unknown?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't really give an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is no such circumstance, because none exists, it's an impossibility, both in fact and in law, that a reasonably prudent forensic pathologist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you asking him? Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, again, Your Honour, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's so obvious, Mr. Ostojic. It's the way you phrased it, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll restate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dunjic, remind us how many years of forensic pathological experience you have, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can look at his grey hair. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's okay, fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should have read his CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did but it would have been leading if I said he had X amount of years, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any event, in any event, Dr. Dunjic, in all seriousness, have you ever seen a forensic pathology report where the cause of death was unknown or unascertainable and yet the manner of death was cited by the pathologist other than in these documents that you've reviewed here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk about two other concepts which is --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you. Dr. Dunjic, let's talk about two other concepts, and that is exhumation and relative or compared to post-mortem examination. Yesterday, early in your testimony on approximately or on page 30, specifically, you said that at first blush, when you look at those reports, they seem essentially acceptable, and then you went on to say that you had "a major objection and that there was omissions by the examiners in the absence of a detailed description". Do you -- and there's more, all observed changes on the corpses in the body. Do you, as a forensic pathologist, when we talk about exhumations and I think it's on page 127 of your report under Roman numeral number 5, you initially state, I'll just -- it's 127, roman numeral 6, actually, and you state, "The standard methods were generally used and the graves were analysed in detail." Do you see that? It's in paragraph 5 in your opinion section, just toward the end of your report. Where it starts, sir, if I can just help a little bit, where it states "the applied methodology of the evacuation and exhumation." Roman numeral 6.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that in that report and I think I mentioned that yesterday, meaning the applied methodology of exhumations as described actually what is done in an exhumation, how the bodies are transported, marked, where they are kept and so on, as well as the process from taking them out from the cold rooms to the actual autopsy itself and then the description of the procedure that is carried out, this is absolutely accurate, and there are no remarks or objections there. This is as far as the procedure goes. Then the reports on the autopsies that I examined are of a certain -- have a certain template. It's a form where all the things that need to be looked at are listed as well as there is a space where the description should be given, so all that I have mentioned so far is standard procedure, and it's all accurate. There are no remarks on that. The remarks are in another part that relate to the pathologist himself, who has taken this particular form and has inspected the body and noted down whatever he noted down. What is actually noted down, what is written down. As I said, as for external and internal and traumatological findings are all separate things. We have a standard that we need to stick to in these collective reports, how this procedure should be carried out, and in these collective reports, the way that was put, you can see that everything was done properly, but the individual reports, and what is said in the individual reports, which is why I asked to see these autopsy reports, there, you can see the points which I remarked on, my objections to these autopsy reports, and this is objective that diagnoses are used, that they are superficial, there are no detailed descriptions and there is a conclusion about the cause of death and death -- the fact of the death itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we do see that obviously, Dr. Dunjic, on the next page of your report. Under that same subsection, on page 128, after you comment on the San Antonio report you find that as you just said it was insufficiently precise or imprecise, there was superficial and that there were arbitrary conclusions made. My question to you is this: What if any effect does this have on the totality in your opinion on the exhumation process that was conducted?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is evident in the autopsy reports and in the things that I mentioned yesterday and today. What I noted is not related to the objections. I just put them there as an illustration to confirm what I said yesterday and the day before and what I said before in my analysis of the individual reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a more precise question. You as a forensic pathologist, when you're looking at that knowing that the exhumations were insufficiently precise, arbitrary and, as you put it superficial, do you have an opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's extremely leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respectfully disagree. First, I didn't even state the question. Second, I can ask this witness on direct if he has an opinion based on factors that he's concluded and whether -- I just don't see how it's leading at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead with your question. Mr. Ostojic is referring to the witness's report, specifically two parts where the same words are used so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dunjic, I was starting to ask you this specific question. As a forensic pathologist, based on a reasonable degree of certainty, when you look at exhumation reports which are insufficiently precise, arbitrary and superficial, what does that cause you as a forensic pathologist to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively, one of the reactions from positions that I'm in, as a professor of forensic medicine is that this was carried out with younger colleagues with not enough experience. This is one of the possible explanations why this was so. Or when I say insufficient experience, what I mean is that people who are not specialised in this work conducting the autopsies. I'm not sure of that, but actually the way the findings are put can lead one to such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, based on your experience, doctor, do you have an opinion whether you would find those reports to be reliable or not, given that you found that they are imprecise, superficial and arbitrary, among other things?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer specifically and I cannot say that this applies to all the locations. I said very precisely in the analysis and pointed out the autopsy reports that were very precise, according to the forensic medicine standards. I did not say that this applied to each one. But I found a large number of such protocols as such and cited them, but for a number of them you can see that they were very precisely done which indicates that they were done by a pathologist with a broad and specialised knowledge and experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, doctor, and forgive me, I wasn't implying that each and every one of the exhumations were done arbitrarily, superficially or without precision, but those that you've identified, my question was just those that you made that conclusion with respect to those exhumation sites, would you find them to be reliable or unreliable, the results or conclusions from those exhumations that you criticised, found deviations, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pointed that out, that these were reports that a person could not rely on or comment on them in a particular way without exceeding one's area of expertise. You can actually give an opinion but the opinion must be based on a fact which as such is very precisely defined and stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me move now to that second subject. We covered a bit here, exhumations, the post-mortem examinations, and I've noticed in your report specifically on pages 35, 36 and peppered throughout the report, where you use the term such as impossible to establish, absolutely arbitrary, incorrect, incomplete and superficial description and you go on on page 37, unclear, incomplete, superficial again, and then ultimately, unprofessional description. End quote. I think if you just look on page 35, 36 and 37 you'll find that just for the sake of time. When you say, sir, it was an unprofessional description, are you saying that your opinion based on a reasonable degree of forensic pathology is that the professionals who rendered these opinions failed to meet the standard of care required of a reasonably prudent forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll restate it, Your Honour because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, there is no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is your -- what do you mean when you make these conclusions? We can go through each one but let's just try to short circuit a little bit. When you reach the conclusion that it's impossible to establish, absolutely arbitrary, et cetera, what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am indicating to you that that report, such as it is, the way it's defined and written, is not checkable and it's impossible to prove, meaning if somebody claims that it's a gunshot wound but has not described it as a gunshot wound then it's impossible to confirm that, just as when we are talking about the cause of death, we are talking about forensic medicine, we cannot perhaps establish if the wound was inflicted before or after death so in that case we can talk about lack of experience or lack of professionalism, when the forensic medicine method of work was not adhered to and then we come to perhaps subjective opinions. So these are some examples that I used to illustrate the objections or remarks I came out with in relation to specific cases. For example, when we are talking about places where we have head injuries that were caused on the scene of death or at point-blank range. This is something where it would be very difficult to state because there would be no finding indicating such a fact. So in some cases, it could -- this could be a personal position, unless the person who drafted the report actually saw for himself when the person who died actually sustained a wound or an injury in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And therefore can you give us an opinion, doctor, as to whether or not that would be considered by you or any other forensic pathologist as being reliable or unreliable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the question is rather vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't think it is, but I'll restate it just so that we could pass and the Court doesn't have to rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are talking about post-mortem examination, and you've given us in your report and your testimony these last two days certain opinions that you found that the pathologists who conducted these post-mortem examinations conducted them with certain deviations or defects, if you will, with all due respect to them, that you've highlighted for us, such as impossible to establish, meaning the external, internal and traumatological findings, that you also find that they are absolutely arbitrary, also arbitrary, also incorrect, et cetera, et cetera. With respect to those findings, sir, you as a reasonably prudent forensic pathologist, do you consider these post-mortem examinations to be reliable or unreliable?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In short, according to my criteria, they should be considered unreliable. The fact is that the corpse exists. Everything else that should have accompanied the autopsy report is imprecise, incorrect, superficial, so that I was not able to draw a conclusion from such a finding. I cannot deny the fact that there is a corpse, but this part, I cannot accept, and this is precisely why I commented on individual cases and individual segments. The same thing applies to the collective reports that I commented on. I did not put objections on the entire report because in three sentences, this and this was said that does not, for example, correspond to the individual reports. I just gave an illustration in order to be able to confirm the individual autopsy report. In some segments of the collective reports, there is nothing to object to. These are some facts, assertions. But in some of those, their assertions, some of the pathologists and those who drafted the collective reports showed subjectivity in relation to some conclusion that they reached which is not covered by an adequate finding so that the person reading the collective report, for example, if we are talking about point blank or executions where these would be the last in a series of injuries, well, this is something that cannot be accepted absolutely because there is no medical element that could confirm this. So in that segment of that report, I can consider it personally nuanced and subjective. It's some impression of the person, and a subjective position of the person stated in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I think you told us at page 51, line 7 through 8 that, "A conclusion in an autopsy report has to represent an objective judgement of what has been established by the findings," end quote. And what you're suggesting to us is that it does quite the opposite in these autopsy reports and the material that you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you make a conclusion as to the objectivity or subjectivity of the autopsy reports and do you have an opinion as to whether or not the forensic pathologists deviated from the standard that they should maintain an objective judgement of what has been established based upon the findings, those three that we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can really respond quickly. I think we talked about reliability and not objectivity and I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You dealt with objectivity already, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, yesterday you mentioned on page 48, lines I think 22, the ABCs of professional -- of your profession. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You also went on in the next lines, I think it's lines 1 through 7 to say that when you reviewed these post-mortem examination autopsy reports by the pathologists, you saw nothing, and I'm quoting, "We see nothing but mere statements saying that this is it, and you have to take it for the face value." My question to you, sir, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, is that how pathological reports are supposed to be drafted where there is no bases for the opinions or conclusions that a pathologist reaches and renders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has already made himself clear on these issues and what you are trying to ask him now pertain more to the area of submissions than to questions to this witness. He's already given us --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, there is some, just so the record is clear, there is some specificity to the question but I will I'll move on with the court's instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Dunjic, having reviewed all the reports from the archeologists, anthropologists, forensic pathologists, et cetera, did you find any instance where the -- where those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him put the question first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- where those persons from the OTP actually concluded at any time one corpse having either been the cause of death or a manner of death from a legitimate military combat engagement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour and dear counsel, you're putting me in a position to provide a summary or general assessment of what I did. I will, however, act as a forensic pathologist and I will answer in the following. I precisely quoted all of the documents I had analysed, and I commented on each and every one of them, providing my opinion. Therefore, I cannot speak about it as a whole, since your question was of that nature. I stick by the facts I had analysed, written down, commented upon for each individual case, in terms of autopsy reports and the collective reports I quoted. I cannot draw a conclusion of the type such as you had defined in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Dunjic, I couldn't find any, so I just wasn't sure if you found any. Let me ask you this because earlier today immediately after the last break, I think it's on page 70, you talked about samples being taken from other parts of the corpse, if you will, the hands and all that. Do you know if there was any analysis done to determine if -- and I'm directing your attention specifically to one of the conclusions you have in your report, which is under again page 127, roman numeral 5, did you find any analysis from the forensic pathologists, whether it was a cursory or a detailed review, that they conducted any gunpowder residue examination to determine whether the deceased individual was military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me ask him a question first. Is it possible with the kind of dead bodies in their various stages of either putrefaction or skeletonisation, is it possible to conduct such examinations as firearms residue or gunpowder residue after these bodies have been buried, in particular, and sometimes reburied, Mr. Dunjic, or Professor Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such an analysis would be very difficult to carry out, such as referred to by some of the people involved, and the results obtained in such a way would be highly debatable. However, something that probably was necessary in certain situations was to analyse the traces that could be found in the area of the wound or damage itself. I'm not talking only about external factors of gunpowder, explosion, and residue either on the skin, bones or clothing, but inside the trajectory, the canal. That means that on putrefied corpses it is very difficult to prove, precisely because of the state of decay of the soft tissue. That is why we insist on examining the canal or the trajectory of the word on hard tissue, for example from one end to the other end of the bone. Once a projectile had gone through, not only gunpowder residue may remain but particles of the casing itself. As for gunpowder residue that would be a very difficult thing to do and results may prove unobtainable. However, in those cases in which we have soft tissue preserved as well as the clothing on the corpse, in certain situations, depending on the degree of changes, such analyses should have been conducted. It wasn't done. Therefore, it renders any comment on that impossible. I believe that would be my response. Forensically speaking I agree with what my colleague said, that it was difficult and impossible to do because of the putrefaction changes in particular on skeletonised corpses. But, however, it should have been noted in the autopsy report as something that was not done or was impossible to do. That is all I would like to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 74, just now on line 1 you used the term that you used throughout or in parts of your report, "Debatable." Now, if you could just explain to us what you mean when you say it's debatable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, vague, Your Honour. Can we have a specific situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour, I'll be happy to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at your report, specifically case number 055, 056, 057, 058 and 062, for example, where you use the word "debatable" and you used it specifically on line 1 in answering Your Honour Mr. President's question on page 74 and I just want to have a better understanding of what you mean, sir, when you use the word "debatable" and just because everyone can follow along, I'll ask that it be brought up on e-court. As I said, we could take any one of those, so let's take 58.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What location, please? You mean the cause of death as something that is debatable?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you could just turn to page 56, for example, which is -- of Dr. Dunjic's report 20990, and obviously the several pages before that, and several pages after that, I think I've cited the case number but if we just look back at ERN X004-6156, case number NK 08057 B, and it's under your comment section right before the next case that you've done which is 058, you used the word "debatable."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that it's on e-court so that my learned friends can follow along with us. Again, just so it's clear, it's page 56 of Dr. Dunjic's report and it has the court transcript page number when it was filed as 20990, but any one of those ten pages because I think it's in each of those pages would be adequate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we can find this page quickly. We have found it. Have you found it from the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They are not even looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We trust his answer on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, they have raised the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we just have actually a minute but could you just explain and I'm sorry, it is late so sometimes we get giddy, but can you just tell me, please, when you use the word debatable as you have in your answer to the Court's question, what are you really saying there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under that term, in a number of cases, I meant the following. I tried to be as precise as possible. I wrote down, as in other cases, the cause of death is debatable. I had already explained why and how. I simply referred to the topic of the cause of death that we discussed. That's why I used the word "debatable" in that context. This includes all the cases I referred to as such. And I had elaborated upon that in the preceding chapters when discussing the cause of death. I'm trying to say that I don't want to discuss this case in particular because I had already discussed that previously. I only commented on the segment it referred to. As for the cause of death, I simply wanted to refer the reader back to what I've already said, ante-mortem, post-mortem, practically and theoretically and why we use certain things when discussing that. That is the context of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to have to leave it at that today. Thank you very much, Professor Dunjic. We will continue tomorrow morning. I'm being asked to check with you how much longer, how much more time you require to finish your direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No more than 15 to 20 minutes, if I may. I'll try to look to pare it do you know if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
